reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / WHO Classification of Endocrine Tumours
clinicalPearls: Usually presents as a solitary, slowly enlarging thyroid nodule in a euthyroid patient, more often in iodine-deficient regions and in older adults than papillary carcinoma
The diagnosis of malignancy cannot be made on cytology alone: it depends on histological demonstration of capsular and/or vascular invasion, which requires the whole excised nodule
Cytologically identical to follicular adenoma, so aspiration typically yields an indeterminate 'follicular neoplasm' (Bethesda category) that mandates diagnostic surgery
Spreads mainly by the haematogenous route to lung and bone rather than to lymph nodes, in contrast to papillary carcinoma
Frequently driven by RAS mutations or PAX8-PPARG rearrangement, and molecular testing can help stratify indeterminate nodules

Being a differentiated follicular-cell tumour, it usually concentrates iodine, so radioactive iodine and TSH suppression have a role after total thyroidectomy, with thyroglobulin used for surveillance
Minimally invasive tumours (capsular invasion only) carry a far better outlook than widely or angioinvasive tumours
reference.pathophysiology: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is a differentiated malignancy of follicular epithelium that, unlike papillary carcinoma, lacks diagnostic nuclear features and is instead recognised by invasion of its own capsule or of blood vessels. Oncogenesis commonly involves RAS-family point mutations or the PAX8-PPARG fusion, activating growth signalling while cells retain iodine-concentrating and thyroglobulin-secreting function. Because tumour cells preferentially enter blood vessels rather than lymphatics, dissemination is predominantly haematogenous, producing distant metastases in lung and bone, sometimes as the presenting feature, while regional nodal involvement is relatively uncommon.
additionalDifferentials: Follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma
Benign colloid nodule within a multinodular goitre
Parathyroid adenoma or nodule adjacent to the thyroid
Metastasis to the thyroid from another primary
additionalInvestigations: Neck ultrasound to characterise the nodule and assess the remaining gland
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration reported by the Bethesda system, typically indeterminate
Serum TSH and thyroid function to confirm euthyroidism
Molecular testing of indeterminate aspirates including RAS and PAX8-PPARG
Serum thyroglobulin and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies as a post-operative marker
Cross-sectional imaging or bone assessment when distant, particularly pulmonary or skeletal, spread is suspected
redFlags: Presentation with a pathological fracture or lung nodules indicating haematogenous metastasis
Rapid nodule growth, fixation, or hoarseness suggesting invasion beyond the capsule
Widely invasive or extensively angioinvasive disease on histology
Rising thyroglobulin during follow-up indicating recurrent or metastatic disease
reference.prognosis: Minimally invasive follicular carcinoma has an excellent prognosis approaching that of papillary carcinoma, whereas widely invasive and angioinvasive tumours, older age, and distant metastasis substantially worsen outcome.
pitfalls: Attempting to diagnose or exclude malignancy on aspiration cytology alone, when only histology of the excised capsule can distinguish carcinoma from adenoma
Assuming absence of lymphadenopathy excludes malignancy, given the haematogenous spread pattern
Failing to search for distant metastases in a patient with a bone or lung lesion and a thyroid nodule
Underestimating angioinvasive tumours that appear encapsulated but carry a high metastatic risk
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Total thyroidectomy is the mainstay, following diagnostic hemithyroidectomy that demonstrates capsular or vascular invasion
Administer radioactive iodine ablation for iodine-avid residual or metastatic disease, exploiting the tumour's retained iodine uptake
Suppress TSH with levothyroxine to reduce stimulation of residual differentiated tumour, individualising the degree of suppression to recurrence risk
Undertake surveillance with serum thyroglobulin and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies together with neck ultrasound to detect recurrence
Treat radioiodine-refractory progressive disease with tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as lenvatinib or sorafenib
Manage skeletal metastases with external beam radiotherapy and bone-targeted agents, and pulmonary metastases within a specialist framework
Coordinate care through an endocrine surgery, endocrinology and nuclear medicine multidisciplinary team
